summary: Eritrea lies in the Horn of Africa on the western shore of the Red Sea. It was once an Italian colony and became independent from Ethiopia in 1993; its capital, Asmara, is a World Heritage site for its modernist architecture.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam has been connected with this Red Sea coastal region from very early on: around 615, some followers of the Prophet Muhammad, fleeing persecution in Mecca, crossed the sea to seek refuge with the Kingdom of Aksum, known in history as the “First Hijra.” Thereafter, through Red Sea trade, ports such as Massawa and the Tigre, Saho and Afar peoples of the western and northern lowlands gradually became Muslim, and in the 16th century the Ottoman Empire even controlled Massawa. Today Muslims are distributed mainly in the lowlands and coastal areas.

ranking.name: Eritrean Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In the 4th century King Ezana of Aksum, under the influence of the missionary Frumentius, converted to Christianity, and Orthodoxy has since been deeply rooted among the Tigrinya people of the highlands. The Eritrean Orthodox Church originally belonged to the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, broke away after independence in 1993 and was recognized as autocephalous by the Coptic Church of Egypt in 1998; but in 2006 the government removed Patriarch Antonios, and the church has long been under state control.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the mid-19th century the Italian Lazarist missionary Giustino de Jacobis preached in the highlands and established a Catholic community using the Ge‘ez rite; during Italian colonization of Eritrea (1890–1941), Catholic schools and churches were built in large numbers, and the Asmara Cathedral is a building from that time.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In 1866 the Swedish Evangelical Mission entered Eritrea, establishing Lutheran churches and schools and translating the Bible into Tigrinya. In 2002 the government recognized only four religions, Orthodoxy, Catholicism, Lutheranism and Sunni Islam; Pentecostal and other Protestant groups were banned and their believers were often detained, so the Protestant share is very low.

religion.background: Eritrea lies at the heart of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum, became a Christian country in the 4th century, and was among the first to come into contact with Islam in the 7th century, forming a pattern of Christianity in the highlands and Islam in the lowlands. In the late 19th century European missionaries brought Catholicism and Lutheranism, and from 1890 Italian colonization further extended Catholic influence. After independence in 1993 the government imposed strict controls on religion, allowing only four officially recognized religious groups to operate, with the two major religions roughly half each of the population.

language.official: Eritrea has no legally designated official language; Tigrinya, Arabic and English are the main working languages.

ranking.name: Tigrinya
ranking.description: Tigrinya belongs to the Semitic family, is closely related to the Ge‘ez of ancient Aksum and is written in the Ge‘ez script; it is the mother tongue of the residents of the central highlands, including Asmara. After Ethiopia annexed Eritrea in 1962 and forcibly promoted Amharic, it provoked national resistance; after independence in 1993, Tigrinya became the main working language of government, the media and education.

ranking.name: Tigre
ranking.description: Tigre likewise derives from the Ge‘ez branch and is spoken in the northern and western lowlands and along the coast, mostly by semi-nomadic Muslims. Because it was long transmitted orally, its written form came late; after independence the government promoted mother-tongue education, and only then did Tigre begin to be used for teaching in primary schools.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: Arabic arrived with Red Sea trade and Islam, and the Rashaida, who migrated from the Arabian Peninsula in the 19th century, speak it as their mother tongue. During the war of independence the Eritrean Liberation Front used Arabic as an important language, and after independence Arabic and Tigrinya became de facto co-working languages, used in Muslim communities and in religious education.

language.history: Eritrea’s Semitic languages derive from the Ge‘ez of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum; Ge‘ez was later retained only in church liturgy, while Tigrinya and Tigre branched from it. Italian colonization from 1890 to 1941 left a number of Italian loanwords; after World War II, Britain administered the territory for ten years, from 1952 it was federated with Ethiopia, and after its annexation in 1962 Amharic was forcibly imposed. After independence in 1993 the government advocated equality of nine ethnic languages, with primary education in the mother tongue, Tigrinya and Arabic as the main working languages, and English used in secondary and higher education.

ranking.name: Zigni (spicy beef stew)
ranking.description: A red stew of beef or lamb slow-cooked with plenty of onion, tomato and spicy berbere spice powder, eaten with injera.
ranking.history: Zigni is Eritrea’s national dish and belongs to the same tradition as Ethiopia’s “wat” stews. Its key spice, berbere, has chili as its base, and chili is native to the Americas and reached the Horn of Africa only in the 16th–17th centuries through Portuguese and Ottoman trade networks, showing that the modern form of this dish is a product of global trade. It is often served on festivals, at weddings and at weekend family meals, with everyone gathered around one large injera and tearing off pieces to eat by hand.

ranking.name: Injera
ranking.description: Teff flour is fermented with water and then cooked on a large flat pan into a big thin pancake covered in small holes, slightly sour and springy.
ranking.history: Teff is a grain native to the highlands of the Horn of Africa, cultivated in this region for thousands of years, drought-tolerant and suited to the highland climate, and was one of the staple grains of the ancient Kingdom of Aksum. Eritreans call injera “taita,” and it is both plate and utensil, as people tear off a piece and wrap stew to put in the mouth. Sharing a single injera symbolizes closeness and unity, and the host often feeds a guest a mouthful by hand, called “gursha,” as a mark of respect.

ranking.name: Shiro (chickpea stew)
ranking.description: Roasted chickpea flour is cooked in water with onion, garlic, tomato and spices into a thick, paste-like stew, eaten with injera.
ranking.history: Eritrean Orthodox believers fast from animal products every Wednesday and Friday and during Lent, with more than a hundred fasting days a year, so shiro, made from legumes, has become the most important vegetarian dish. Chickpea flour keeps easily and cooks quickly, and during the long war of independence from 1961 to 1991 it was also an important ration for fighters and civilians. It is Eritrea’s most common home dish, loved equally by Muslims and Christians.

ranking.name: Ful (stewed fava beans)
ranking.description: Fava beans are stewed until soft and mashed, then mixed with oil, onion, chili, tomato and yogurt, and often eaten with French-style bread; it is a common breakfast.
ranking.history: Ful originated in Egypt and Sudan, and Egyptian control of Massawa in the 19th century (1865–1885), together with long-standing Red Sea trade, brought the dish into Eritrea. Eritreans often eat ful with the bread left from the Italian colonial period, showing the meeting of several foreign food cultures. It is the most popular breakfast in the cafés and small restaurants of Asmara and is also common during Ramadan.

ranking.name: Fit-fit
ranking.description: Injera or bread is torn into small pieces and mixed into a sauce cooked with berbere chili paste and spiced butter (tesmi), sometimes with minced meat or yogurt added.
ranking.history: Fit-fit was originally invented as a frugal dish to use up the previous day’s leftover injera, showing how a food culture built on injera as a staple avoids waste. It is common in both Eritrea and Ethiopia, often eaten as breakfast or a late-night snack, and during fasting periods a vegetarian version is made with vegetable oil. Today it also appears on restaurant breakfast menus and is a familiar home flavor to Eritreans.
